More data does not always lead to better decisions. In behavioral economics and decision psychology—popularized by researcher Barry Schwartz—people generally fall into two camps: maximizers and satisficers.

Maximizers feel compelled to evaluate every available option to guarantee the absolute best outcome. Satisficers, by contrast, define clear, non-negotiable standards upfront and commit as soon as an option meets them. While maximizing sounds ideal on paper, research consistently shows it leads to analysis paralysis, slower execution, and greater post-decision regret.

For investors, founders, and corporate leaders, the cost of over-optimizing is measurable. Waiting for complete certainty in volatile markets means missing entry windows, stalling product launches, and burning cognitive bandwidth on marginal gains.

Effective decision-making isn't about lowering standards—it's about setting explicit thresholds before you start looking, knowing which calls are reversible, and moving forward once the fundamentals check out.
